title: “LOVE ALWAYS TRUSTS”—SO WHY DOES LOVING THEM KEEP DESTROYING YOU?
paragraphs: “LOVE ALWAYS TRUSTS”—SO WHY DOES LOVING THEM KEEP DESTROYING YOU?
Does Christianity Require You to Trust Someone Who Keeps Hurting You? What 1 Corinthians 13:7 Actually Says May Set Someone Free Tonight.
There is a sentence in the Bible that has comforted millions of people.
And wounded some of them.
Not because the Bible was wrong.
Because somebody used it wrong.
“Love always trusts.”
Maybe those words were handed to you while your heart was still bleeding.

Maybe someone lied to you, betrayed you, manipulated you, humiliated you, cheated on you, abandoned you, controlled you, or repeatedly broke promises—and when you finally became afraid to trust them again, somebody reached for 1 Corinthians 13.
“Love always trusts.”
So you stayed.
You believed another promise.
You ignored another warning.
You silenced another question.
You wondered whether protecting yourself meant you were bitter.
You wondered whether asking for accountability meant you were unforgiving.
You wondered whether noticing the pattern meant you lacked faith.
And perhaps the most painful part was this:
You started wondering whether God Himself expected you to keep handing someone the weapon they kept using to wound you.
If that is where you are, please keep reading.
Because Scripture does command Christians to love.
Scripture does command Christians to forgive.
Scripture does command us to reject bitterness, vengeance, hatred, and unforgiveness.
But Scripture never commands you to call darkness light.
Jesus never taught that forgiveness requires pretending nothing happened.
And biblical love is not the same thing as unlimited interpersonal trust.
Those distinctions matter.
Especially when somebody has repeatedly hurt you.
Paul's actual words in 1 Corinthians 13:7 are:
πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει.
Panta stegei, panta pisteuei, panta elpizei, panta hypomenei.
Literally, the verse carries the repeated force of:
Love bears all things.
Believes all things.
Hopes all things.
Endures all things.
The phrase commonly translated “believes all things” is:
πάντα πιστεύει — panta pisteuei.
The crucial verb is πιστεύει — pisteuei, from pisteuō.
It can carry the sense of believing, trusting, having faith, or placing confidence in something.
But here is where context becomes everything.
Paul cannot mean that Christian love requires believing every statement another human being makes regardless of evidence.
Why?
Because only one verse earlier Paul tells us:
“Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth.”
Love and truth are not enemies.
Biblical love does not require abandoning discernment.
Love does not demand that you believe a lie simply because the liar says, “If you loved me, you would trust me.”
That is not 1 Corinthians 13.
That is manipulation wearing a Bible verse.
Imagine someone has lied to you ten times.
They come back an eleventh time.
“I promise.”
You want desperately to believe them.
Your heart remembers who they used to be—or perhaps who you hoped they would become.
But something inside you hesitates.
Then guilt whispers:
Love always trusts.
And suddenly discernment begins feeling like sin.
But listen carefully.
The same Jesus who commanded extraordinary forgiveness also said:
“Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”
He did not say:
Be innocent and therefore naïve.
He joined innocence with wisdom.
A Christian heart can remain tender without becoming gullible.
You can refuse hatred without refusing reality.
You can forgive somebody while recognizing that their character has not yet become trustworthy.
You can pray for somebody while refusing to participate in their destructive behavior.
You can desire their restoration while requiring evidence of change before restoring the same level of access.
Because forgiveness and trust are related...
but they are not identical.
Forgiveness is something Christians are commanded to extend.
Trust is relational confidence.
And relational confidence can be shattered.
Jesus Himself gives us a breathtaking picture in Luke 17:3:
“If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
“If your brother sins, pretend it didn't happen.”
He said:
Rebuke him.
That means biblical love can confront.
Biblical love can name wrongdoing.
Biblical love can say:
“This hurt me.”
“This was wrong.”
“This cannot continue.”
“I forgive you, but something must change.”
The Jesus who teaches forgiveness is the same Jesus who makes room for confrontation.
That should free somebody from years of unnecessary guilt.
Because perhaps you were taught that a loving Christian never confronts.
Jesus disagrees.
Perhaps you were taught that boundaries automatically mean bitterness.
Scripture does not say that.
Perhaps somebody told you that forgiveness means immediately returning a relationship to exactly what it was before betrayal.
Scripture does not say that either.
And perhaps somebody keeps demanding your trust while refusing the very repentance that could begin rebuilding it.
That is not reconciliation.
That is entitlement.
Real repentance does not merely say:
“Why can't you get over it?”
Real repentance begins saying:
“I understand why what I did damaged your trust.”
It does not demand instant restoration.
It accepts accountability.
It stops blaming the wounded person for bleeding.
It begins producing fruit.
Because biblical repentance is more than regret over consequences.
It is a turning.
And this is where grace becomes astonishing.
Christianity does not teach us to permanently imprison people inside their worst moment.
The Gospel exists precisely because sinners can change.
Liars can become truthful.
Adulterers can repent.
Addicts can be transformed.
Abusers of power can surrender.
Prodigals can come home.
Hard hearts can become flesh again.
People who destroyed trust can, through genuine repentance and the transforming work of Christ, become different people.
That is grace.
But grace is not pretending transformation has happened when it hasn't.
Grace tells the truth about sin precisely because grace believes Jesus can redeem the sinner.
Think about Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine hearing Peter swear that he did not know the Man he had promised never to abandon.
What a scandal.
Yet Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to tell Peter betrayal was harmless.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
The man who denied Jesus became a man commissioned to feed His sheep.
That is not cheap grace.
That is transforming grace.
Jesus did not merely erase Peter's scandal.
He rewrote Peter's future.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you are not the person who was betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you manipulated somebody.
Maybe you repeatedly broke someone's trust and then became angry because they could no longer believe you.
Maybe you have been quoting “love always trusts” because facing what you did feels unbearable.
Then hear this with hope:
Jesus Christ is not asking you to manipulate someone into trusting you.
He is inviting you to repent.
There is a difference.
You do not need to defend the old you.
You need Christ to crucify it.
Stop demanding that someone ignore the fruit of your past behavior.
Start asking Jesus to produce new fruit in your life.
Confess what you did.
Stop minimizing it.
Stop blaming the person you wounded for responding like someone who was wounded.
Accept consequences where consequences remain.
Seek forgiveness without demanding control over the response.
Then walk faithfully.
Tomorrow.
And the next day.
And the day after that.
Let integrity become ordinary.
Let truth become your language.
Let humility become visible.
Let repentance become more than an emotional speech.
Trust may return slowly.
Perhaps painfully slowly.
But genuine change does not need manipulation to prove itself.
Fruit eventually speaks.
And to the person who has been hurt...
there is another danger you must guard against.
Pain can teach discernment.
But pain can also become a prison.
Someone betrayed you, so now nobody gets close.
Someone lied, so everybody becomes suspicious.
Someone abandoned you, so you leave first.
Someone weaponized your vulnerability, so you buried tenderness somewhere so deep that even people who genuinely love you cannot reach it.
That is not healing either.
The person who hurt you should not be allowed to become the architect of every relationship you have afterward.
Jesus wants more for you than that.
Christian wisdom does not say, “Trust everybody.”
But neither does Christian healing say, “Trust nobody.”
It says something infinitely safer:
Trust Christ completely.
Let Him teach you how to love people truthfully.
Humans can fail.
Jesus does not.
People can change overnight.
Christ is faithful.
People can promise forever and disappear tomorrow.
Jesus said He would never leave nor forsake His people.
Your deepest trust was never meant to rest upon the flawless performance of another sinner.
It belongs to God.
And when that foundation is restored, something beautiful happens.
You can forgive without becoming foolish.
You can love without enabling.
You can hope without denying evidence.
You can establish boundaries without hatred.
You can say “no” without becoming cruel.
You can leave room for restoration without manufacturing reconciliation.
You can pray:
“Jesus, I forgive them. I refuse revenge. I refuse hatred. I refuse to let bitterness become my master. But give me wisdom about what access this person should have to my life.”
Sometimes love opens the door.
Sometimes love waits to see fruit.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love says, “You need help.”
Sometimes love creates distance.
Sometimes love refuses to participate in another person's sin.
Sometimes love welcomes the genuinely repentant person home.
And sometimes love continues praying from somewhere safer.
None of those decisions should be made merely from fear, anger, pressure, or a single slogan pulled out of context.
They should be brought before Jesus.
Because Christ is not merely interested in saving relationships.
He is interested in saving people.
Sometimes preserving the illusion of peace allows sin to continue unchecked.
Sometimes the most loving thing somebody can hear is:
“No more.”
No more lying.
No more manipulation.
No more hiding behind Scripture.
No more demanding forgiveness while rejecting repentance.
No more calling consequences “unloving.”
No more using God's grace as permission to remain unchanged.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping us become comfortable versions of the same people.
The Gospel announces death and resurrection.
The old life dies.
A new life begins.
Christ forgives sinners—and Christ transforms sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did not minimize our sin.
Look at Calvary and you discover how seriously God takes evil.
Our rebellion was not brushed aside.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
And yet look again.
Because Calvary simultaneously reveals how fiercely God loves sinners.
Jesus took what guilty people deserved.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Justice and mercy met.
Truth and grace kissed.
The scandalous were offered redemption.
The guilty were offered forgiveness.
The spiritually dead were offered life.
That is why Christianity can look directly at betrayal without surrendering hope.
Jesus specializes in resurrection.
But resurrection requires something to die.
Maybe tonight it is your bitterness.
Maybe your denial.
Maybe your manipulation.
Maybe your obsession with getting revenge.
Maybe your insistence that somebody trust you before you've become trustworthy.
Maybe your belief that forgiveness means becoming available for another wound.
Maybe your fear that boundaries make Jesus disappointed in you.
Bring it to Christ.
All of it.
You don't need another inspirational slogan.
You need Jesus.
And perhaps somebody else needs this truth tonight too.
Someone is sitting alone wondering whether Christianity requires them to walk back into the same cycle because “love always trusts.”
Send this privately to someone who would never admit publicly what they are going through.
Because emotions become confusing when old wounds reopen, and you may need to return to this truth:
Forgiveness does not require pretending evil was trustworthy.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't disappear quietly.
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain.
But sometimes three honest words become the moment someone stops pretending.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, pointing you back to Scripture, helping wounded believers find their way toward Jesus, and reaching people who desperately need the Gospel, consider becoming one of the people who helps keep this mission moving.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Pray.
Then act according to your conscience before God.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about real wounds and complicated lives.
But whether you ever give one cent or not, never confuse the messenger with the Savior.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church cannot save you.
Religious performance cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
Follow Jesus.
And let Him begin rewriting what you thought could never be redeemed.
Because maybe the deepest question was never:
“Do I have to trust the person who keeps hurting me?”
Maybe the question beneath the question has always been:
“After everything that happened...is there still Someone I can trust completely?”
Yes.
His name is Jesus.
People may break promises.
People may break hearts.
People may even misuse Scripture while doing it.
But Christ remains faithful.
And when human betrayal leaves you afraid to trust again, remember this:
You don't have to reopen every door to prove you have forgiven—but never let the person who broke your trust convince you that Jesus will break His too.
